chapter_theme: Poems 241-260 are poems of death and what follows it: laments for patrons (Ay, Saththan of Ollaiyur), an old man's lament for his youth, a king's lament for his wife, widows who choose the pyre or live on alli and greens, wives alone with a husband's body in the wilds, two poems on an ascetic who was once a seducer, the vetchi raiders and their toddy, and a karanthai hero whose name passes onto a stone.

241.reading: Andiran, the cool-garlanded giver of sturdy chariots to suppliants, is told as arriving among the gods: at the cry that he is coming, the leather-covered drum sounds in the palace of the tall one with the thunderbolt in his great hand, and a cheer goes up in the sky.
241.nuance: Death is never named. The lament is turned inside out into a welcome: the only thing said of the king is that he gave chariots, and that alone is what the heavenly hall announces, so his giving is presented as his passage. The god is named only by his weapon (வச்சிரத் தடக்கை).

thinai_evidence.note: a patron's death told as his reception in the sky, a lament (கையறுநிலை) that porul 2.24 sets under kaanchi

242.reading: With Saththan of the strong spear dead, who overcame warriors so that his manhood showed, no young man wears the mullai, no bangled woman plucks it, the bard does not draw it down with the curved arm of his lute to wear it, and the bard-woman does not adorn herself with it; the poet asks the flower whether it still blooms in the land of Ollaiyur.
242.nuance: The four refusals name his whole household of dependents: the young fighters, the women, the bard and the bard-woman. The question to the flower is a reproach: the land goes on producing what no one now has the heart to use, so the flower that should be ornament becomes the measure of loss.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead chief, spoken to a flower that blooms on as if nothing had happened

243.reading: An old man remembers the untaught youth in which he offered flowers to a doll of packed sand, joined hands with the girls bathing in the cool pond, swayed and embraced with a guileless crowd, climbed the low marutham branch at the ford and leapt into the deep water with a splash while those on the bank gasped, and dived to bring up sand; he pities it, and asks where it is now for him, propped trembling on a ringed staff, a very old man of few words broken by coughing.
243.nuance: The colophon names the poet after the ringed staff of line 12, so the poem supplied its own author's name. The youth is praised as கல்லா, untaught, and its worth lies exactly in that: no secrecy, no calculation. The colophon files a lament for one's own youth under கையறுநிலை, which elsewhere is grief for a dead patron.

thinai_evidence.note: the passing of youth into old age, the impermanence that kaanchi is about

244.reading: A fragment: the bees no longer hum over the bards' heads, the bard-women's forearms no longer shine with bangles, and the suppliants too... (the rest is lost).
244.nuance: The bees are absent because the bards wear no flowers, and the bangles because no gold is given: both are signs of a patron's death read through what his dependents no longer have. Whose death it was is lost with the rest of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the household of performers stripped of garlands and bangles, the aftermath of a patron's death

245.reading: The king asks what measure grief can have, however great, if it lacks the strength to take life: his young wife has been laid on a bed of bright flame on a pyre of seasoned wood in the bare, kalli-grown open ground and has died there, and he still lives; what kind of thing is this?
245.nuance: The grief is turned against itself: it is called great and then shamed for being too weak to kill. The colophon calls it கையறுநிலை, but by the Tholkappiyam's list it is the husband's தபுதார நிலை; the poet is the king himself. Line 1 opens on யங்குப், which reads as யாங்குப் with its first letter damaged.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband's lament for his dead wife, the தபுதார நிலை of porul 2.24

246.reading: Perunkoppendu, queen of Bhoothapandiyan, rebukes the many elders who will not say 'go' but hold her back with 'stay': she is not one of the wretched widows who, untouched by fragrant ghee, eat leaf-wrapped hand-squeezed rice cooked with white sesame paste and tamarind and boiled velai greens, and sleep on gravel with no mat; let the great pyre of dark logs be hard for them, but for her, since her broad-shouldered husband is dead, a lotus pond full of open flowers and the fire are one.
246.nuance: Her list of what she will not become is the most exact account of a widow's observances in the anthology: no ghee, leaf-wrapped rice, sesame paste and tamarind, boiled greens, a gravel bed. She calls the elders' counsel பொல்லாச் சூழ்ச்சி, so the poem sets a wife's will against the wisdom of the assembly. By the Tholkappiyam's list the situation is பாலை நிலை (the wife who enters the fire with her husband); the colophon files it as ஆனந்தப் பையுள்.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife who will enter her husband's pyre, the பாலை நிலை of porul 2.24

comparisons.tenor: the whiteness of the ghee
the pyre's fire

247.reading: In the burning ground, lit by the drill-fire that foresters kindled with dead wood the elephant brought, where a herd of gentle deer is roused from its sleep and female monkeys scamper in a courtyard where spirits dwell, the queen with wet hair falling down her dark back and eyes of great sorrow looks at the great burning ground and wavers: she who was seldom alone in her husband's wide, guarded mansion, where the drum's eye never slept, now turns her back on her youth, her sweet life trembling.
247.nuance: The burning ground is drawn with forest life (the elephant's wood, the foresters' fire, startled deer, monkeys), so the wildness of the place is set against the guarded, drum-loud mansion she has left. Whether she is about to enter the fire or to live on as a widow the poem does not quite say; line 9 (சிறுநனி தமியள் ஆயினும்) and the sense of சீக்கும் in line 4 are hard.

thinai_evidence.note: a widow at the burning ground giving up her youth

248.reading: A widow pities the small white water-lilies: when she was young they were her garment of leaves, and now that her husband of great wealth is dead they have become the poor alli food she eats on painful days, refusing the proper hour.
248.nuance: One plant spans her whole life: its leaves dressed the girl, its seeds feed the widow. The pity (அளிய) is spoken to the lilies, but it is her own change she is measuring.

thinai_evidence.note: a widow's life after her husband's death, the தாபத நிலை of porul 2.24

249.reading: Where the aaral fish hides in the mud, the vaalai leaps at the surface and turtles turn up at the rasping taḍāri drum as fishermen trample the flame-flowered fields together and scoop up roe-swollen varaal and bright kayal, the lord of that wide land once ate his food in company with many; now, as he has gone to the high world, his young wife of restrained chastity and fine brow clears a small space with an ash-smeared winnowing basket and smears it with cow dung and with the tears of her eyes that will not stop weeping.
249.nuance: The abundance of the first seven lines and the shared meal of line 8 are set against the small cleared patch where the widow now eats alone: the poem turns on நெருநை (yesterday) and இன்றே (today). Line 11 is broken in our text, so what she does as he enters the high world is lost.

thinai_evidence.note: the widow's mourning rite after her husband's death

comparisons.tenor: the roe-swollen varaal fish
the bright kayal fish

250.reading: The poet tells the prosperous mansion that it has become desolate: its gate once held back suppliants with rich, sizzling rice and relish and its cool fragrant pandal stopped the tears of patrons, and now, since the father of tuft-headed sons who hold white rice and ask for sweet milk has gone to the lonely burning ground, it holds a wife who has cut her hair, put off her small bangles and eats alli food.
250.nuance: The house is addressed, not the widow, and food runs through every stage: the feast that stopped suppliants at the gate, the widow's alli, and the small sons still asking for milk. The children, who do not yet know what has happened, carry the poem's last weight.

thinai_evidence.note: the house and wife after the householder's death

251.reading: The man who, in a spacious house like a painting, made doll-like girls with small bangles grow thin until their ornaments slipped, is seen now bathing in the waterfall of a tall hill of bamboo, tending a fierce red fire with wood the forest elephant brought, and drying the matted locks that hang down his back.
251.nuance: The poem is built on the before and after of one man, and the only detail of his former life is the women who pined for him. The same elephant-gathered firewood that lights the pyre in 247 here feeds the ascetic's sacrificial fire. Line 3's கண்டிக்கும் is unusual (the old first-person plural கண்டிகும், 'we have seen', is expected).

thinai_evidence.note: the victory of the ascetic's life (தாபத வாகை)

comparisons.tenor: the spacious house
the girls with small bangles

252.reading: The ascetic who now plucks soft-leaved thaali, his matted hair dulled and changed in colour like the thillai tree from standing under the roaring white waterfall, was once a hunter who snared, with a net of words, the gentle peacocks that move about the house.
252.nuance: The hunter is the past and the ascetic the present, so the poem reverses the moralist's suspicion that an ascetic may be a hunter in hiding. His weapon was speech (சொல்வலை), and the women are not named but drawn as peacocks of the house. Line 5 ends with a stray closing quotation mark.

thinai_evidence.note: the ascetic set against his former life as a seducer

comparisons.tenor: the ascetic's dull matted hair
the man's former wooing of the women of the house

253.reading: A wife speaks to her husband who has fallen in the wasteland: let him not grieve for her any more; since he came as the young men with strong-strapped garlands rejoiced, how is she to go among her kin raising an empty hand without bangles, pale as a young bamboo stripped of its sheath; let him tell her his word.
253.nuance: The bare arm is the public sign of widowhood, and her question is how to carry it among her people. Line 3 (நாகாஅல் என வந்த மாறே) is hard and the sense of her first line turns on it.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife alone after her husband's death on the road, the முதுபாலை of porul 2.24

comparisons.tenor: her pale arm without bangles

254.reading: The speaker addresses the warrior who fell in the middle of the wasteland, not rising to meet the attack, his chest embracing the earth, while the young and old went off to other lands: if, raising her pale empty bangle-less hand among the kin, she carries the word that the young man has come to this, what will become of his mother, who daily, without tiring, praised him, saying that her son's wealth and greatness were to them like the bird-filled plenty of the fruiting banyan at the edge of the town.
254.nuance: Lines 3 to 4, on the pale empty hand raised among the kin, repeat 253 lines 4 to 6 almost word for word, so the bare arm raised among kin was a set image of this thurai. The grief is displaced onto the mother's praise, quoted in her own words: the banyan full of birds is a son who feeds many. The comparison's marker is the அற்று of தற்றே, an அன்ன-type form.

thinai_evidence.note: a death in the wasteland and the news that must be carried home

comparisons.tenor: the son's wealth and greatness to his family

255.reading: A wife over her husband's body in the wilds says that if she cries out she fears the tiger and if she tries to embrace him she cannot lift his broad chest; she wishes on lawless Death, which did him this harm, a great trembling like her own, and asks him to take hold of her wrist with its wave-ridged bangles and walk a little, so they may reach the shade of the hill.
255.nuance: Each of the first two lines closes a way of grieving (crying aloud, embracing); the last asks the dead man to do the impossible, take her hand and walk. Death is called அறனில், without justice, a charge laid against Death itself rather than fate.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife alone with her husband's corpse in the wilds, the முதுபாலை

comparisons.tenor: Death, cursed to tremble as she does

256.reading: A widow asks the potter of the wide old town to take pity on her too, who came with her husband through many wastelands like the small white lizard that clings to the spoke of an axled cart, and to make the burial urn in the wide grove of broad flowers wide enough for both.
256.nuance: The lizard on the spoke goes wherever the wheel turns without moving itself, which is how she describes her travels with him; the request is practical (make the urn wider), and the burial urn rather than the pyre is the rite named.

thinai_evidence.note: a widow who came through the wastelands with her husband asks to share his grave

comparisons.vehicle: அச்சுடைச் சாகாட்டு ஆரம் பொருந்திய சிறுவெண் பல்லி
comparisons.tenor: the wife who travelled with her husband

257.reading: Who is he, poor fellow, this man like a pebble in a sandal, with thick calves, a fine belly, a broad chest, fresh eyes, a beard of coarse hair set like rows of sticks, and cheek hair hanging below his ears, carrying a bow? He did not ride far from town in a chariot or take the forest as his fort, yet in the morning, watching the backs of the enemy's departing herd, he pointed with his hand, counted them slowly and turned them with his bow; and many though they are, what are they to him, who never hears the daily sound of the churning stick in a pot that shows no white?
257.nuance: The poem begins as if puzzled by a stranger (யார்கொலோ, அளியன்) and ends by showing why he is pitied: he takes herds by the score, yet his own pot never shows the white of curd, because he keeps none. The seizure is made without chariot or fort, by a man counting cattle on his fingers.

thinai_evidence.note: the seizure of the enemy's herd, the deed vetchi is named for

comparisons.tenor: the young raider, a constant vexation to the enemy
the coarse hair of his beard

258.reading: The sweet toddy, matured until it bursts like the old fruit of the thorny kaarai, was drunk first by the young man with the thin beard at the head of the gathered company; he ate raw meat, wiped his wet hand, greasy with fat, on the back of his bow and went into the empty land, and before one round can be drunk he will bring a great herd to fill the outskirts of the town; so the speaker tells the woman to keep the old-mouthed jar from everyone's touch, for that lover of toddy, dusty with eagerness, can also be fierce.
258.nuance: The toddy is not his pleasure but his advance pay: the jar is to be kept for him because he will bring back the herd before the others finish drinking. The comparison's marker is ஏய்ப்ப, a போல-type word. Line 10 (ஆதரக் கழுமிய துகளன்) is hard; the sense of eagerness is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: a raider who will bring the herd home, honoured with the first toddy (உண்டாட்டு)

comparisons.tenor: the matured toddy

259.reading: The speaker warns the warrior with the bright sword at his side and the wrought anklet not to go, not to go, without seeing the ambush of strong-bowed fighters who stayed hidden, heads covered, in the leafy great forest when the herd with its bulls was driven back: may his heart do well, though it is set on the cattle that leap and spring like an old possessed pulaitti.
259.nuance: The poem is a warning, not a praise: the recovered herd may be bait, and the hidden bowmen are the danger. What the simile compares is not certain: the leaping cattle, or the hero's eager rush toward them; முதுகுமெய் (possessed) is itself a rare compound.

thinai_evidence.note: the pursuit to recover a seized herd, the deed of karanthai

comparisons.tenor: the cattle leaping and springing

260.reading: The poet tells a bard whose tuning slips into the mourning mode, whose heart fails, who saw his wife's loosened hair as an omen, worshipped the god in the kalli shade of the salt waste and came hungry and weeping asking 'shall I not see him?', to hear how the prosperous one stands: whether he would have eaten under his protection or wakes at night in distress, both now lie close at hand; the hero appeared at the alarm of the near village, gathered his town's long herd, crossed the flood of arrows with the drum for a raft, won, killed, made the raiders let go, and as the moon escapes the sharp fang of the snake that seized it, the many cows with their calves escaped the raiders' hands and came back with his fame; then, like a snake shedding its skin, he went to the world hard to reach, his body stayed there shaking with arrows like a target post shaking with its pole on the steep bank of a forest stream, and his name, risen until high fame could hold no more, is on the stone in a narrow path no one else takes, under a cloth canopy, crowned with the fine feathers of the gentle peacock.
260.nuance: The hero is split three ways at his death: the self goes like a snake from its skin, the body stays behind shaking with arrows like a target post, and the name moves onto the stone. The bard's omens at the start (the slipping tune, the loosened hair) are confirmed rather than answered, and the poem gives the bard the hero-stone in place of a patron. The marker of the snake simile is மான, a போல-type word.

colophon.thurai: கையறுநிலை செருவிடை வீழ்தல்; கையறு நிலையுமாம்; பாண்பாட்டுமாம்; பாடாண் பாட்டுமாம்

thinai_evidence.note: the hero recovers the herd and dies, and is set up as a stone, the karanthai deed and its sequel

comparisons.tenor: the hero crossing the arrow-storm with only his drum
the herd escaping the raiders' hands
the hero leaving his body for the other world
the hero's body shaking with arrows

links.note: Two kaiyarunilai poems on the death of Ay Andiran: 240 stays at the pyre and the scattering bards, 241 looks to the drum of the heavenly hall.
links.teaches: Read together, the pair shows that a lament for a patron could face downward to the hungry dependents or upward to his welcome among the gods, and that the heavenly version is offered as consolation for the earthly one.

links.note: 241 presents Andiran's giving of chariots as what announces him in heaven; the Kural says giving is good even if there were no higher world.
links.teaches: The Kural's hypothetical answers a real habit of praise: poets like this one tied giving to a welcome in the sky, and the couplet deliberately cuts that tie so that giving no longer needs the reward.

links.note: Both picture old age on a staff, but the Naladiyar calls youth faulty and the wise renounce it in infancy, while 243 calls its untaught youth precious and grieves for it.
links.teaches: The same image of the old man on a staff serves the Jain moralist as a warning against enjoying youth and the Sangam poet as proof that youth was the best of life, so the later book is arguing against a value the older poetry held.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 157 calls the mourners who burn the body and bathe unjust for returning to life; 245 is a mourner who burned his wife and is appalled that he still lives.
links.teaches: The king's poem complicates the Tirumanthiram's charge: survival after the pyre is shown not as forgetting but as grief's own failure to kill, which the survivor feels as shame.

links.note: The queen of 246 refuses the widow's life of greens and alli; the widow of 248 lives it and pities the lilies that now feed her.
links.teaches: Placed side by side, the two poems show that the widow's diet was a known, codified life that one woman could choose to bear and another could scorn as worse than the pyre.

links.note: Both are filed as ஆனந்தப் பையுள: 246 gives the queen's refusal in her own voice, 247 shows a widow at the burning ground from outside, wavering.
links.teaches: The resolve that 246 voices without a tremor is seen in 247 from the outside as hesitation and fear for one's young life, so the same thurai holds both the heroic and the frightened face of the same choice.

links.note: Both name alli as the widow's food (அல்லி உணவின், அல்லிப் படுஉம்).
links.teaches: The repeated alli food shows a fixed sign of widowhood shared across poets, which 250 sets against the house's former feasting and 248 against the girl's lily-leaf garment.

links.note: The Kural likens the false ascetic to a hunter hiding in a bush to snare birds; 252 says this ascetic really was a hunter, snaring women with words, before he became one.
links.teaches: Both use the hunter and the snared bird for the ascetic, but in opposite order: for the Kural the hunter hides inside the ascetic, for the Sangam poet the ascetic has replaced the hunter, so the same image can accuse or praise a renunciant.

links.note: Two poems by the same poet on the ascetic's life: 251 sets the seducer against the ascetic at the fire, 252 names his past as hunting with a net of words.
links.teaches: The pair shows the poet working one contrast twice, with the second poem turning the past from the women's pining to the man's own art of capture, which makes the renunciation a giving up of skill as well as pleasure.

links.note: Both have the bare, pale, bangle-less hand raised among the kin (வளையில் வறுங்கை ஓச்சிக் கிளையுள்).
links.teaches: The near-identical line in poems by different poets shows that the widow's raised empty arm was a fixed formula of the முதுபாலை thurai, used in 253 for the wife's own shame and in 254 for the news she must carry to the mother.

links.note: The Kural's mother rejoices more at hearing her son called worthy than at his birth; 254's mother praises her son daily, and the speaker dreads her hearing of his death.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem shows the other side of the Kural's maxim: the mother whose joy rests on hearing her son praised is the one whom the word of his death will strike hardest.

links.note: Both are spoken by a wife alone with her husband's body in the wilds: 255 tries to move him to the hill's shade, 256 asks the potter for an urn wide enough for two.
links.teaches: Taken in order, the two widows move from refusing the death (walk a little, she tells the corpse) to arranging to share it, which shows the range of response that the முதுபாலை thurai held.

links.note: The Kural says shame turns her back on drinkers; in 258 the toddy jar is reserved for the raider as an honour before his deed.
links.teaches: The pairing shows that drinking was an honour of the warrior's rite (உண்டாட்டு) in the older poetry, so the Kural's chapter against liquor is rejecting a heroic custom, not only a private vice.

links.note: The Kural says a death that is really existence is hard to achieve save for the skilled; 260 shows the hero's body left shaking with arrows while his name passes onto the stone.
links.teaches: 260 gives the Kural's abstract paradox a concrete form: the 'death that lives' was a practice with a body left on the bank, a stone set in a narrow path, and a name crowned with peacock feathers.

links.note: 259 warns the karanthai warrior against the ambush as he chases the herd; 260 tells of a karanthai warrior who recovered the herd and died of the arrows.
links.teaches: Read in order, the warning of 259 and the hero-stone of 260 give the two ends of the herd-recovery: the danger seen in advance and the death it brings, which is why the recovery's praise ends at a stone.

links.note: 246's speaker is the queen of Bhoothapandiyan; the colophon of Akananuru 25 names Bhoothapandiyan as its poet, whose hero vows 'let my life suffer' at parting.
links.teaches: Through the colophons, the akam poet who wrote a lover's promise not to stay away is also the husband whose wife refused to outlive him, so the anthologies let a convention of inseparable lovers stand beside one recorded marriage.

new_concepts.gloss: the helpless grief of those left behind after a patron's or hero's death
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons use the word: கையறுநிலை for 241 to 245 and 260

new_concepts.gloss: widowhood and its observances: cut hair, no bangles, alli food, the gravel bed
new_concepts.label_source: label is ours; the colophons call the situation தாபதநிலை, and the poems name its signs (அல்லி உணவின், கூந்தல் கொய்து, வளையில் வறுங்கை)

new_concepts.gloss: the hero-stone raised for a warrior who died, bearing his name
new_concepts.label_source: label is ours from the usual name; 260 line 28 says the name is on the stone (கல்மிசை யதுவே)

new_concepts.gloss: the seizure and recovery of cattle herds, the deed of vetchi and karanthai
new_concepts.label_source: label is ours; the poems use நிரை (257 line 8, 258 line 7, 259 line 1, 260 line 13)

source_issues: 244: the poem breaks off in line 3 (இரவல் மாக்களும் followed by dots); poet and patron are missing, and thinai and thurai were filled from Duraisamy Pillai. The colophon thinai carries a trailing comma (பொதுவியல்,), copied as it stands.
245 line 1 begins யங்குப், which lacks its first letter; it reads as யாங்குப்.
245: the colophon thurai is கையறுநிலை, but the situation (a husband who has lost his wife) is the Tholkappiyam's தபுதார நிலை (porul 2.24); not an error, but a mismatch of schemes.
249 line 11 has a lacuna (அவன்புக .. .. வரி); the poet field carries a variant name (தும்பி சொகினனார்;தும்பிசேர் கீரனார் என்பதும் ஆம்).
251 line 3: கண்டிக்கும் is unusual; the old first-person form is கண்டிகும்.
252 line 5 ends with a stray closing quotation mark (முன்னே.’), and 253 line 6 and 254 lines 6 and 8 have unpaired quotation marks.
259: the colophon thurai carries a variant in brackets (பிள்ளைப் பெயர்ச்சியுமாம்), given as a second puram_thurai item.
260: the colophon thurai begins கையறுநிலை செருவிடை வீழ்தல், which runs two thurai names together; and the thinai carries a bracketed alternative (பாடாண் திணையுமாம்).
